children: David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research argued that history offers little comfort for a Federal Reserve tightening into an energy-price shock.

Outside of 2022, when households were flush with roughly $2 trillion in pandemic-era fiscal transfers, the central bank has not avoided a recession in the postwar period under those conditions. That warning now sits against a freshly more hawkish policy stance under Chair Kevin Warsh and a Treasury curve that is only about 30 basis points from a 2s/10s inversion—a signal Rosenberg says deserves close attention.

Official and market consensus still treats a downturn as remote. Rosenberg disagrees. He expects a sizable surprise and cautions that the current artificial-intelligence boom, however powerful, does not repeal the business cycle. The early-2000s internet expansion, he notes, likewise failed to override a later contraction.

Prediction markets echo the complacency on the near-term calendar. On Kalshi, a 2026 U.S. recession is priced at just 5.4%. Odds rise to 27.1% for 2027—still a minority view, but a clearer acknowledgment that any payback from tighter policy and higher energy costs may arrive with a lag rather than immediately.

title: Fed tightening into an energy shock has seldomly ended well, Rosenberg Research says
